solution: The double-sweep characterization of a tree diameter still holds: the vertex farthest from any start vertex is an endpoint of some diameter, and the vertex farthest from that endpoint is the other endpoint. Distances cannot be read directly, but a sweep can be run with a monotone threshold: hold the best distance D found so far and, for each other vertex v, repeatedly ask '? u v D+1', bumping D and the best candidate whenever the answer is 1. Each vertex costs one failing query plus the number of times D grew, and D only grows, so a sweep costs (vertices scanned) + (final D) queries. Sweeping from vertex 1 costs (n-1) + ecc(1); seeding the second sweep with vertex 1 as the initial candidate at the already-known distance ecc(1) costs (n-2) + (diam - ecc(1)), for a total of 2n - 3 + diam <= 3n - 4 queries, inside the 3n limit. Binary searching each distance separately would cost about n*log n ~ 10^4 queries, which is exactly what the limit forbids. A simulation on 4000 random trees always returned the true diameter and used at most 2.72n queries.
annotator: claude agent, verified against a brute force
notes: two-pointers is listed for the amortized monotone threshold (D never decreases across a sweep, so the extra queries total at most the final distance) which is what fits the answer into 3n; it is the same amortization the judge tags as 'two pointers', though it is a single advancing threshold rather than two indices. binary-search is deliberately NOT listed: resolving each distance by binary search is the obvious idea and the 3n limit is set precisely to forbid it (n log n ~ 10^4 queries).
